title: Distributed Web Crawler: Complete Architecture
description: Design a scalable, polite web crawler (Googlebot scale) with Mercator Crawl Frontier, DNS caching, SimHash near-duplicate detection, and Bloom filters.

data.text: Design a distributed, production-grade web crawler capable of fetching, parsing, and storing 1 billion web pages per month across 10+ million distinct internet domains. The system must discover new links recursively from seed URLs, strictly respect robots.txt and host politeness delays, eliminate near-duplicate content via locality-sensitive hashing (SimHash), avoid spider traps and infinite URL loops, and feed structured document representations into downstream search engine indexers.

terms.definition: A dual-queue scheduling architecture combining Priority Queues (importance/PageRank) and Politeness Queues (one per host) to prevent overloading any single target web server.
Enforcing a minimum interval (e.g. 1 request every 2 seconds per domain) and honoring `Crawl-delay` and `Disallow` directives from robots.txt.
A 64-bit locality-sensitive fingerprinting technique where similar documents produce hashes differing by fewer than 3 bits (Hamming Distance ≤ 3), identifying scraped or near-identical pages.
A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether a URL has already been queued or visited, running in RAM with zero disk I/O.
Pathological website structures (e.g. infinite calendar links, dynamically generated query parameters) that trap crawlers in endless recursive fetch loops.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: URL Discovery & Traversal: Traverse the web recursively starting from trusted seed domains and sitemaps
Politeness & Robots.txt: Parse, cache, and respect domain robots.txt rules and crawl-delay policies
Near-Duplicate Detection: Detect and drop syndicated copies and template variations using 64-bit SimHash
URL Normalization: Canonicalize URLs (resolve relative paths, lowercase hostnames, strip tracking tokens)
Content Extraction: Strip HTML boilerplate to extract title, main body text, meta tags, and outgoing hyperlinks
Raw Storage: Store raw HTML snapshots in standard WARC format in object storage for offline reprocessing

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 1 billion pages per month (~400 pages fetched/sec average, 2,500/sec peak)
Storage: ~500 TB raw HTML storage per month; ~50 TB extracted text and link graph data
Politeness Guarantee: Never hit the same host IP more than once per configured delay window
Extensibility: Pluggable parser modules for PDF, images, and headless browser rendering (Playwright)
Robustness: Isolate worker crashes caused by malformed HTML, infinite redirects, or slow server tar-pits

data.text: The architecture employs the classic Mercator Crawl Frontier pattern. The Frontier decouples priority scheduling from politeness enforcement. Distributed fetchers communicate with dedicated DNS caches and feed raw content into a decoupled parsing and deduplication pipeline.

data.text: To ensure a target host is never overwhelmed, the Fetcher checks the Host Delay Heap before emitting an HTTP request, updating the next allowed timestamp immediately after download completes.

faqs.question: Why is DNS resolution a major bottleneck for web crawlers?
faqs.answer: Fetching millions of pages across millions of distinct domains requires millions of DNS lookup queries. Standard OS DNS resolvers are blocking and slow (tens to hundreds of milliseconds per lookup). The crawler must use a high-concurrency custom asynchronous DNS resolver with an in-memory cache holding IP addresses for 24+ hours, bypassing recursive root lookups.

faqs.question: How do you detect and escape Spider Traps?
faqs.answer: Spider traps are websites with endless generated URLs (e.g. `site.com/calendar?year=2099` or recursive directories `site.com/dir/dir/dir`). Mitigation: (1) Impose a strict maximum URL path depth (e.g. max 8 segments), (2) Limit total pages crawled per domain, (3) Use URL length caps (e.g. max 256 characters), and (4) Detect repetitive URL segment patterns via regex heuristics.

faqs.question: How does a Bloom Filter track billions of crawled URLs in memory?
faqs.answer: Storing 1 billion full URL strings (average 80 bytes) requires 80 GB of RAM. A Bloom Filter with 1 billion elements and a 1% false positive rate requires only ~1.2 GB of RAM (approx. 9.6 bits per element). If the Bloom filter says a URL is "new", it is guaranteed to be new with 0% error; if it says "already seen", there is a 1% chance it was missed, which is an acceptable trade-off for internet crawling.

faqs.question: How are client-side rendered Single Page Applications (React / Vue) crawled?
faqs.answer:
Standard HTTP GET requests only receive empty `
` shells. Crawlers maintain a tiered processing pipeline: 90% of pages are parsed using fast static HTML extractors (Cheerio / Lexbor); URLs identified as JavaScript-heavy SPAs are routed to a headless browser worker pool (Playwright / Chromium) running in headless containers to evaluate scripts and render DOM.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Mercator Crawl Frontier separates URL priority scheduling from per-host politeness queue management
Delay Heaps strictly enforce minimum intervals between requests to protect web servers from accidental DDoS
SimHash 64-bit fingerprints detect near-duplicate pages with modified ads, headers, or timestamps
In-memory Bloom filters track billions of seen URLs with under 2GB of RAM consumption
Custom async DNS resolver caches eliminate network lookup latency as a crawler bottleneck
data.takeaway: Scalable web crawlers succeed by prioritizing politeness and resource efficiency: in-memory Bloom filters and SimHash engines filter out redundant work before distributed fetchers touch remote servers.
